newsitem.title: INDIA: Foreign-owned nuclear plants welcome - India officials.
newsitem.headline: Foreign-owned nuclear plants welcome - India officials.

text.p: India's top atomic energy officials said on Saturday they will not oppose foreign ownership of nuclear power plants in the electricity-starved country.

"We have no problem on 100 percent foreign ownership (of atomic plants) as long as they operate within our rules and regulations," Y.S.R Prasad, managing director of state-run Nuclear Power Corporation (NPC) said.
"If the government thinks it's beneficial we have no problem," he told Reuters by telephone from Kakrapar, 300 km (186 miles) north of Bombay in western Gujarat State.
A Japanese business newspaper report on Saturday quoted Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda as saying India would allow full foreign ownership of nuclear power plants.
Government officials in Delhi could not confirm the report.
Analysts said the Japanese newspaper may have misinterpreted remarks by Deve Gowda on the government's policy on foreign investment in power generation.
"This is too premature," said Dr R. Chidambaram, chairman of India's Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) in Bombay. "I cannot comment on the report."
He said the AEC was not against foreign participation in nuclear power generation.
"Let somebody come with a proposal. We'll look into it," he said. "We have a strong indigenous (atomic energy) programme. We're happy to add to it."
India has nine nuclear reactors generating a total of just under 2,000 MW of power, officials said.
The demand for power was growing by an average of nine percent every year, and India needed to add 142,000 megawatts of power generation by 2007, Deve Gowda said recently.
Officials say roughly 40 million rupees ($1.1 million) are needed to create one megawatt of capacity.
Analysts and officials said opening atomic power plants to foreigners was not feasible because of rigid controls on transfer of nuclear technology.
"No where in the world is the nuclear sector opened to foreigners," said NPC's Prasad. "Not to my knowledge."
India is not a signatory to the Non-Proliferation Treaty and the United States has been opposing Russia's planned sale of two light water nuclear reactors to India.
"That's (the Japanese newspaper report) not correct," said one official who asked not be named. "The Atomic Energy Act needs to be amended for even tie-ups with local partners."

He said only the state sector was allowed in nuclear power generation under the statute and there was no move to open up the sector to foreigners, but tie-ups with local private sector firms were possible.
Joint ventures with state electricity boards and Indian firms like Larsen & Toubro and Bharat Heavy Electricals which make specialised components were likely to happen, he said.
